articles.text: Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson were formally announced as new members of Piedmont School Board on Monday, December 19. They were sworn into office by City Clerk John Tulloch at a regularly scheduled City Council meeting held in the Community Hall instead of City Hall. The venue change allowed for a reception afterwards in celebration of new and departing elected officials from the School Board and City Council. articles.text: The Piedmont Public Works Department received feedback last week from AC Transit on Piedmont’s proposed bulb-outs and changes in bus stops on Oakland Avenue. The City’s initial bulb-out plan involved the net loss of 10 parking spaces; the modified plan has three. If the City is unable to address these concerns in a new draft, it would amount to a net loss of four. AC Transit expressed concern that buses in the westbound (downhill) direction on Oakland Avenue at Jerome Avenue would project across the intersection with Latham Street. “I am very optimistic that the City will reach an agreement with AC Transit, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “These back-and-forth iterations are typical, and it’s realistic that we’ll resolve them in January.” In the meantime, the City continues to work with residents to develop a plan which is agreeable for those affected. Gonzales said he has received requests from some residents for the City to paint the affected curbside areas in order to make it clear where the new bus stops will be. When the initial plan for bulbouts on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito Avenues was approved by the City on October 4, 2021 and presented to the public recently on November 1, “there was pushback from many parties,” confirmed Gonzales. In addition to permanent bulbouts – where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer – the plan provided for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. There was opposition to the loss of parking spaces which would result from relocating bus stops on Oakland Avenue near the affected intersections. Accordingly, the City created a modified bulb-out plan. The new plan addresses a majority of the concerns voiced by residents and involves a net loss of three parking spots – one on El Cerrito Avenue in the downhill direction, and two at Jerome Avenue. “As we work with AC Transit to maintain the modified plan while keeping to their safety guidelines,” said Gonzales, “we’ve also made sure to be very proactive in working with those affected by this plan.” Residents with questions about the bulb-out plan may e-mail Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or call 510-420- 3061. articles.text: The American Red Cross will have a blood drive on Saturday, December 24, from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Blood donations are fewer during the winter holidays due to travel, illness, and weather, but the need for blood is constant. Volunteer donors are the only source of blood for trauma and cancer patients, accident and burn victims, people with blood disorders, and more. Blood donors must be at least 18 years old (16-17 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, and wait a minimum of eight weeks between making donations. To make an appointment, visit redcrossblood.org/give.html/finddrive and use the sponsor code “Piedmont”. To learn more about donating blood, visit donateblood.org/ faqs/#who-can-donate. Parental consent forms can be found online at bit.ly/3HF715S.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s highly-anticipated White Elephant Sale will return next year beginning with a preview sale on January 29. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest and best rummage sale,” is organized and operated by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and a legion of volunteers, many working throughout the year to make the sale a success. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the museum to support its art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. The sale has many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The preview sale begins at 12 p.m. on Sunday, January 29. Visit https://museumca.org/event/ white-elephant-preview-sale/ to purchase tickets and to learn how to donate.

articles.text: Renovation of the steps connecting the Piedmont Community Hall with Guilford Avenue will begin on January 4. The Public Works Department issued a notice earlier this month to proceed with the project. The $155,000 renovation project was approved by City Council on September 6, 2021, with the understanding that $55,000 of the cost will be funded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Garden Club. Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales estimated that work could be completed in mid-March. “The main priority of this project is safety,” he stated. The city will replace the current steps — which are currently wooden railroad ties of varying sizes — with colored concrete steps and landings, and add metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings. Further additions will include benches, trees, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor to accommodate for groundwater runoff. The Highland/Guilford Steps project plans can be found at bit. ly/3jlK65z, and all City projects out for bid can be found at piedmontplanroom.com. articles.text: Dear PUSD Community: The Holiday Season is here and so much has happened in a month. The district is moving along with the Superintendent Search and community engagement has been completed. In addition to parent, staff and community meetings with the search firm, over 400 individuals completed a survey identifying qualities they would like to see in the next superintendent. The position has been posted and applications will be brought to the Board on February 1 for review. Thank you to everyone for your feedback and assistance in this process. In our School Board community engagement meetings in October, there were parents who felt strongly that rigor and excellence needed to be addressed in the District’s Vision, Mission and Core Values. But what became clear was we all have different definitions of what those values are and how to represent them both in the district and classroom. Does that mean that Piedmont needs to have a certain number of Advanced Placement courses? Does this mean we need to hit a certain mark on State standardized tests? Finally, does rigor and excellence go beyond academics to include social and emotional welfare as well as equity and inclusivity? Getting everyone on the same page is important. To do this, I will be meeting with teachers, administrators and the Superintendent’s Community Advisory Committee to develop an operating definition of rigor and excellence. I will then bring parents into the conversation through several community meetings. Following this dialogue, I will bring to the Board a plan of what rigor and excellence looks like in Piedmont. My goal is to have all stakeholders on the same page and operating under the same definitions. This will become part of a foundation on which we can build and sustain as our district moves forward under the next superintendent. Yesterday, the state released data as part of its accountability reporting system known as the California School Dashboard. The Dashboard is an online tool to help communities identify strengths and weaknesses and pinpoint student groups that may need support. In its sixth year, it reports status on multiple measures of academic and school climate. The Dashboard also focuses on the state priority of closing the performance differences among student groups’ (e.g. race/ethnicity, socioeconomically disadvantaged, English Learners [ELs]) performance. Piedmont continues to demonstrate excellence across multiple measures. With the impact of the pandemic changing the landscape of learning, communities are encouraged to consider these results a new baseline and to reflect and engage with their districts in moving forward to support all students. You can review the dashboard at Caschooldashboard.org. PUSD’s results will be presented to the Board on January 11. We just completed our 1st Interim Budget Report. The report gives us a clearer picture of where our finances are. After giving 7.5% salary increases, a $1,500 one-time bonus and an increase in health care benefits to all staff, we were still able to receive a positive certification. A positive certification means that we are able to meet all of our financial obligations this year and the two subsequent years. You can read more about the background of the report at Simbli. eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/ Attachment.aspx?S=3603037 3&AID=398174&MID=17392 and view a slidedeck from Wednesday’s Board presentation at Docs.google.com/presentation/d/1CXXcsIMG3BhE9GYQ1E70ZGnPNhZ8h9mb/edit Over the past six months, I have enjoyed meeting with the many amazing organizations that work tirelessly to support our students and staff. I want to take a moment to especially thank the Piedmont Education Foundation that has impressed me beyond belief. Its impact on PUSD can be seen on every campus and in every classroom, and felt by every student and staff member. As its 2022 Giving Campaign comes to a close this month, I invite you to consider making a donation and see the difference it can make. Visit Piedmontedfoundation.org/donate for more information. Finally, as Winter Break approaches, I ask for your help in continuing to provide a safe environment for students and staff. With COVID cases on the rise, we are asking families to test their students prior to returning to school on January 9. Schools will be distributing tests to all students next week. Please plan to test on January 7-8 and report any positive cases on the District’s COVID self reporting form at Tinyurl.com/pusdgotcovid and on Primary. I wish you all a happy and safe Holiday season. Enjoy your break and we’ll see you in the New Year! Sincerely, Donald Evans Interim Superintendent Saturday, February 11. and early ticket sales. coffee, and cocktails.

articles.text: Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans On Wednesday, December 14, community members gathered at the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a discussion with Piedmont School District Interim Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans and Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The Giving Campaign team facilitated and hosted the event, which focused on an overview of PUSD funding sources and expenses, and the financial challenges that the district faces. Emily Chang Stull, an award-winning author and Bloomberg producer and host, moderated the event. Dr. Evans highlighted the unique nature of what Piedmont schools offer students compared to many other public school districts, thanks to community fundraising efforts like the Giving Campaign. “If you go up and down the state (of California), you don’t see fully structured art programs,” he said. “You don’t see structured music programs or technology programs. You don’t see fully operational libraries. Even in some of the highest achieving districts, you will not see all those things…like you see here.” Ruth Alahydoian presented information about how the state funding model works and the expenses involved in running PUSD. “It was so illuminating,” said Giving Campaign co-chair Katie Sharafi. “California gives us only 50% of what we need to operate our schools. The rest we need to find through local sources and fundraising.” Alahydoian also highlighted the importance of reflecting community priorities in funding decisions. “The dollars that we get in donations… it’s important that we spend it as people ask us to spend it,” she noted. Piedmont Education Foundation’s Heather Frank shared information about how the district allocates funds raised by PEF. “Every year, we convene a grants committee that includes a representative from every parent’s club and support group in the district, along with community and PEF board members, the district superintendent, assistant superintendent, and CFO,” she said. “The committee reviews grant spending from the prior year and then determines what community priorities are for distributing funds for the upcoming year.” Questions from the audience ranged from how the district prioritizes areas for funding cuts to the most significant upcoming expenses for the district. Superintendent Evans noted that healthcare costs for PUSD employees CFO Ruth Alahydoian continue to skyrocket and are completely out of the district’s control. Dr. Evans, who has worked in public school districts of all sizes throughout California, feels that Piedmont is unique in the strength of its teaching community. “I am so grateful for what we have here,” he said “Our PUSD teachers are really invested in their classroom and their kids and so committed to their work. That is not true everywhere. What we have here is really exceptional.” He noted that while this year’s 7.5 % teacher raise (made possible by last year’s Giving Campaign fundraising and state distributions) was much higher than raises given by many other districts, the district needs to remain competitive with benefits as well. “To…keep teachers, and give the salaries we want to give them, you have to cut! And what goes out are those things… (art, music, and STEAM programs) that really define us here, that we take for granted.” As the 2022 Giving Campaign comes to a close, it has raised just short of $3 million. But as much as the amount, the team is focusing on participation – parent participation is still under 50%. “Every dollar counts,” says Sharafi. “But getting the community involved is what we’re most focused on right now.”

articles.text: Volunteers at Chabot Space & Science Center do incredible things. They assist educators in workshops to inspire students, run scientific demonstrations to educate visitors and donate their time every Friday and Saturday night to offer free telescope viewing to the public. One rockstar, Gabrielle Stewart, is a Chabot Observation Deck volunteer and UC Berkeley student. She has discovered more than 450 supernovae since February this year, and recently made a particularly rare find on August 1. In the constellation Ophiuchus (the Serpent Bearer), a Type 1a supernova awaited its discovery. With a magnitude of around 19, it wasn’t visible to the naked eye. You’d need a powerful telescope to see it, like the 36-inch reflector on Chabot’s Observatory Deck. For Stewart, this exploding star jumped off the page in photos from the 48-inch telescope at Palomar Observatory near San Diego. What makes this discovery so unique is the fact that this supernova’s brightness is enhanced by gravitational lensing – where a massive object, like a galaxy, has bent the light on its long-distance journey to Earth. Similar to what a lens would do, this effect has made the supernova appear brighter than it normally would. This is only the third such object ever discovered, and the first in six years. A team of astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope was able to capture a picture of the supernova. The lensing is what creates an image that appears to be four objects. Now officially designated SN Zwicky, around these parts we’ll be referring to this discovery as Gabby’s Supernova. Volunteer at Chabot Join a dynamic team dedicated to creating a fun and interactive science experience. No science or astronomy background needed, just a willingness to inspire and educate visitors of all ages about our Planet Earth and the UniChabot Observation Deck volunteer and UC Berkeley student Gabrielle Stewart spots the Supernova Sn Zwicky. verse. If you are comfortable interacting with the public, enjoy engaging children and adults, and have eight hours of your time to give per month, consider becoming a volunteer at Chabot Space & Science Center. articles.text: The Piedmont Diversity Film series will return on January 19 with a free screening of Through the Night. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!” PLEASE JOIN US AS WE CELEBRATE

articles.text: On a cold Christmas Eve in 1818, pastor Joseph Franz Mohr walked the three kilometers from his home in the Austrian village of Oberndorf bei Salzburg to visit his friend Franz Gruber in the neighboring town of Arnsdorf bei Laufen. Mohr brought with him a poem he had written two years earlier. He desperately needed a carol for his Christmas Eve midnight mass that evening. He hoped his friend Gruber, a school teacher who also served as the church’s choir master and organist, could set his poem to music. In a matter of a few hours, Franz Gruber composed the “Stille Nacht” melody for Mohr on that night of December 24, 1818. Flooding of the nearby Salzach River had put the church organ out of commission, so Gruber composed the music for guitar accompaniment. A few hours after Gruber finished the composition, he and Mohr stood before the altar at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf to perform the work. A local choir sang the new composition, breaking the silence of that “stille nacht.” Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. articles.text: If you want to watch some great basketball this winter, head to Binks Rawlings Gym in Piedmont. The Highlanders’ girls’ team was just named the top-ranked team in SportsStar Magazine’s North Coast Section rankings. The No. 1 spot came after PHS notched one of its biggest regular season wins in the last decade with a 60-56 victory over previously No. 1 ranked ArchPerseas Gioukaris is a guard with tough on-ball defense and speed in transition. bishop Mitty of San Jose. In addition to its core of Trinity Zamora, Maddie Hill, and Natalia Martinez, the three lead players throughout last year, a major part of Piedmont’s 6-0 start to the season is the addition of three transfer students. Eva Levingston, Perseas Gioukaris, and Adrienne Blackwell, all seniors, they are making their debut at PHS. In addition, junior Samantha Smith is scheduled to play her first game for PHS against California High this Friday, December 23. Both Levingston and Gioukaris were on the roster last season but had to sit out a year as active players as they waited to be cleared after transferring. They rooted from the bench as Piedmont finished as runners up in the league, in the North Coast Section finals, and advance to the second round of the Div. 2 State Playoffs. All that has only made them eager to do their part on the court. “Honestly, last year was very hard for Perseas and I to sit out. We worked out in the summer coming into last season and were really anxious to play. Sitting on the bench and helping out in practice, sort of as a coach during games. gave me a different perspective,” said Levingston. This is our season and we’re coming for more. Watching those tight games last season was tough because you want to help out. I was very proud of my team,” added Gioukaris. Levingston has already proven a contributor in the low post and as a ball handler. Coach Gardere describes her as a “Draymond Green” type of player. “Bryan says I’m like the Draymond Green on the court. I love being aggressive, and at the same time getting the ball to my teammates,” said Levingston. Levingston comes to Piedmont after playing at St. Joseph in Alameda as a freshman and at Alameda High as a sophomore. Gioukaris is very much the sparkplug described by coach Bryan Gardere. She may be one of the smallest players on the court, but she’s one of the fastest. Her vertical leap makes her an aggressive rebounder to go along with skill as a defender. “I’m very aggressive,” confirmed Gioukaris. “I talk more on the defensive side than offensive. I’m a defensive player first, but I like to push the ball up the court fast.” She played at St. Joseph as a freshman and sophomore. Blackwell is proving to be a skilled shooting guard who can knock down 3-pointers and also drive to the basket. “It’s great to be on this team. We have a target on our backs, and I think we can keep that No. 1 spot with our ability and skillForward Eva Levingston is a key player on Piedmont’s No. 1 ranked team. set,” said Blackwell. She played at St. Mary’s in Stockton as a freshman and at Santiago High in Corona as a sophomore and briefly as a junior before having shoulder surgery. “I’m bringing defensive energy, great communication, and leadership. It feels great to be on the court, I’m also coming back from injury so it’s really a relief,” said Blackwell. articles.text: Messi finally leads Argentine to the championship What a dramatic and amazing World Cup this was. In the end, Argentina captured its first title since 1986 and Lionel Messi solidified himself as the greatest player of the modern generation. Sunday’s f inal between Argentina and France eventually became one of the best World Cup Finals of all time. Completely outplayed by Argentina in the first half, Les Bleus stormed back from a 2-nil deficit, and again from a 3-2 disadvantage in overtime to force a penalty kick shootout of the ages. It became just the third championship game to reach penalties. The early ones were Brazil vs, Italy in 1994, and Italy vs, France in 2006. There were so many illustrious and awe-inspiring moments from this year. Here’s a recap of some of the best. • Lionel Messi cements his legacy Lionel Messi has now done it all; he is a 10-time La Liga winner at Barcelona, a winner of Ligue 1 with Paris St. Germain last year, winner of seven Cope del Reys, a four-time Champions League winner, winner of the Copa America, and now finally, at age 35, is now a World Cup Champion. He scored seven times in this year’s tournament, one behind France’s Kylian Mbappe, and bagged two goals in the final against France. He made the case for the greatest of all time. • Kylian Mbappe revives France Kylian Mbappe, at age 24, was extraordinary in only his second World Cup, He won the Golden Boot award as the leading scorer in the Cup with eight scores, including the first ever hat trick in the finals. He personally revived France after halftime when down 2-0, for a 3-3 tie late in the second period of overtime vs. Argentina. Mbappe is clearly the next great generational talent. Following their win over Spain, Morocco players tossing manager Walid Regragui into the air became one of the most memorable images of this year’s games. • Croatia knocks out No. 1 Brazil Everyone knew walking into the quarterfinals that Brazil was the hands-down favorite, perhaps of the entire tournament with the No. 1 seed. But Croatia had other plans, and relied on its defense to force penalty kicks against the Canaries. It was the same blueprint that helped Croatia advance to the Finals in 2018. Ronaldo’s time with Portugal this World Cup was less than anticipated and only polarized his diminishing product. Going into the games, Ronaldo bad-mouthed Manchester United in a shocking interview. It wasn’t the glorious ride into the sunset Ronaldo envisioned. • Saudi Arabia upsets Argentina Argentina’s World Cup didn’t start as anticipated, losing 2-1 to Saudi Arabia in the opening game on November 22. The Argentines became the first team since Spain in 2010 to lose their first group stage match to eventually lift the trophy. Saudi Arabia fans went viral following the match, asking Where is Messi? They may have not made it out of the group stage, but that upset will live on forever. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside to see the 16-acre estate lit up for holidays. The non-profit historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. Take photos with Santa on December 23 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Afterwards view a dozen festooned Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. Last year, the team installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in the early to mid-1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/. unique pieces for you & everyone on your list! ®

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece Wuthering Heights in a new play by Emma Rice. The play is showing onstage now through January 1. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead performs the lead role as Catherine. Her theater credits include Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), and Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/Liverpool Everyman). Liam Tamne will perform the role of Heathcliff. His extensive discography includes The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane). To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ wuthering-heights/. Berkeley Rep is located at 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Call the box office for tickets at (510) 647-2949, or purchase online at www.berkeleyrep.org.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, will be performed one more week at War Memorial Opera House, with a final show on December 27. This new adaptation is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers within the company to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by a live orchestra that performs Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani — all played by a group of three musicians. The Scenic Design is by Michael Yeargan, costume Design is by Martin Pakledinaz, lighting Design is by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older; no children under age three will be permitted. The ballet runs two hours with one intermission. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. articles.text: The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn verges of being a heartwarming allegory about a mysterious man named Noah Dearborn (Sidney Poitier) who lives alone on a bucolic farm on the outskirts of a small southern town. He is a gifted carpenter, woodworker, generous to a fault, and seems ageless. soon becomes clear that the denizens of the town keep Noah’s presence a well-kept secret, understanding that it’s his preference to live quietly, go about his work, and be left undisturbed. Actually, in countless ways, his life is so spare and timeless, it seems as if the 20th century has passed him by. And so it has, that is until a cohort of land developers arrive and decide that in order to build a shopping center they need Noah’s acreage. Driven by greed, they set up an office in town and send slick and fashionable Christian Nelson (George Newbern) out to pay Noah a visit, prepared to make him an offer for his property that, given the amount, he certainly cannot refuse. Of course, Noah does that very thing: he insists he has no interest in selling his farm, no matter the offer. Nelson points out that Noah could retire, move into town and relax in his golden years. But all Nelson hears in response is a polite “no.” He returns to his office suite and discusses the result with his Mary-Jane Parker and Sidney Poitier in The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. partners, searching for a scheme to get the property, deciding that perhaps there’s a way to get Noah declared mentally incompetent; after all, who in his right mind would turn down the well-over market price they are prepared to pay? Nelson, whose fiancé, Dr. Valerie Crane (Mary-Louise Parker), is a psychologist, gets the idea for her to drive down from the city and pay Noah a visit, the intent being to evaluate him professionally and determine if he is unable to manage his own affairs. Which she does. What nelson is unprepared for is the magic that defines not only Noah, but his farm, especially his residence, which is the second floor of his weathered barn. Valerie is smitten with Noah and grows suspicious regarding her fiance’s plan. And so the story develops, filled with charming moments and outstanding performances by Poitier and Dianne Wiest. She was nominated for an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress, delivering a superb portrayal of Sarah McClelland, a neighbor who lives just down the road from Noah and constantly searches for reasons to have him repair something while thanking him with a homemade pie. And no surprise, Mary-Louise Parker who, in her role as Valerie, displays an abundance of talent. The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. Directed by Greg Champian. Starring Sidney Poitier, Dianne Wiest, Mary-Jane Parker. I hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 1999. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: They were a dynamic duo. Each was a star in the musical firmament, but oh, so different. One of them had a very quiet demeanor. He dressed in black and was known as “the man in black”. The other was much more flamboyant. Perhaps you are thinking of Johnny Cash as the man in black and the more flamboyant musician as Elvis Presley (“Elvis the Pelvis” as he was known). They had a friendly rivalry and even tried to imitate each other. Nothing could be funnier. Elvis’s rock and roll music wasn’t for Johnny Cash and vice versa for Cash’s country music. But… History frequently repeats itself, so let’s go back. The names are different, but the story is familiar. This time we’re talking about classical musicians. The original “man in black” was violinist-composer Arcangelo Corelli and the flamboyant character was the famous German composer George Frederick Handel. Corelli was a rather somber guy and, like Johnny Cash, he liked the low registers of music. He had good connections despite a rather sordid past. In some ways, Presley was quite a bit like George Frederick Handel. Both traveled a lot, wore flashy clothes and were binge eaters. Let’s go back to Rome in 1706. Corelli was rehearsing a composition by Handel. He was having some trouble because of the high register. Handel was present at the rehearsal and became annoyed. Having an assertive nature, he walked up to Corelli and said: “May I borrow your violin? Let me show you how the music goes.” After Corelli got his violin back, being very diplomatic, he said: “Maestro Handel, you must excuse me. I just don’t understand this modern music.” Keeping this story in mind, feel free to investigate Johnny Cash imitating Elvis and listen to some of the seasonal music by Corelli and Handel. articles.text: Crazy Rich Asians is a highgloss romantic comedy, based on the best-selling novel by Singaporean author Kevin Kwan. The story is familiar fare: Nick (Henry Golding), a handsome and successful Asian born New Yorker, brings his girl friend, Rachel (Constance Wu), a Chinese American university econ professor, to his home in Singapore for his best friend’s wedding. What he fails to tell her, though they’ve dated for more than a year, is that he is a scion of one of the wealthiest families in Southeast Asia. They are, without hyperbole, crazy rich. Actually “crazy rich” doesn’t begin to describe the incredibly high-thread-count wealth Nick’s family possesses, a reality that at first stuns, then takes Rachel’s breath away, given that she comes from a modest background and was raised by a hard-working single mom. Recall that in every solid romcom there has to be a roadblock (often comedic) to the couple’s union. In Crazy Rich Asians it is quickly obvious that Nick’s family is a matriarchy wherein his mother, Eleanor (Michelle Yeoh), and his grandmother, Ah Ma (Lisa Lu), steadfastly believe in endogamy and are both committed to sabotaging the couple’s relationship. Not only does Eleanor’s mien suggest her displeasure, but her barbed-tongue rejection of Rachel is voiced with a quiet, almost malevolent hurtfulness. And it is with dripping sarcasm that Nick is reminded by his mother that his girlfriend is Chinese-American with the emphasis on “American.” Michelle Yeoh, Henry Golding and Constance Wu in a sceen from Crazy Rich Asians. It is soon obvious that Rachel – a generous, kind-hearted woman – is overwhelmed not only with the family’s intimidating wealth (I would argue that this lily is far too gilded) but with the countless cultural cues that she can’t quite sort out and which contribute to her sense of unease. Some might call it culture shock lite. Clearly, Nick, in all his good-natured naiveté, has failed to prepare her for what she will have to absorb. What distinguishes Crazy Rich Asians from its antecedents is that the cast is 100 percent Asian, a fact that has been lavished with praise given that Asians are underrepresented in Hollywood. Here is a film that clearly attempts to right this deficit and mirrors much of the discussion that took place when Black Panther was released. Crazy could have been set in any city where the stereotypical conceits of wealth and social class – old money vs. nouveau riche – are concerned. The essential story is pretty much universal. Regarding the outcome, well, in most rom-coms the basic question posed is, “Will love conquer all?” You can, of course, guess at the ending, which brings to mind the Cinderella fairytale. Crazy Rich Asians. Directed by Jon M. Chu. Starring Constance Wu, Henry Golding, Michelle Yeoh. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv.

articles.text: Ignore those who might say that Five Feet Apart relies on a bevy of “sick-lit” tropes. That’s lazy criticism. All narratives rely on the familiar and the vagaries of the human condition. The good ones find new and nuanced ways to construct characters and plots that are compelling. This film does that, intending not only to emotionally reach the audience – in this case the demographic is teen/tween – but it is also meant to educate regarding a harrowing, incurable disease known as Cystic Fibrosis. The setting of Five Feet Apart is a large urban hospital somewhere in the U.S. Stella Grant (Haley Lu Richardson), 17-18, has just returned to what is called the “CFer” ward for what she stoically refers to as “tune-up.” This is not her first visit, for she has chronic CF. She is spirited, resilient, and quick to smile, and she suffers from this incurable, rapacious respiratory disease with a sincere, direct understanding of her circumstances. Mere decades ago, children born with CF likely did not live past their tenth year. Now, medicine and research pushes the expanding edges of the envelope ever outward, well beyond that first decade. Hence adolescents such as Stella are fully cognizant of the challenges that confront them. Stella’s room is hospital cheerful, with a med cart and books and a full bulletin board of getwell cards. Always nearby is her portable oxygen machine that is connected by a plastic tube that is hooked around both ears and inserted in her nose. Monitoring Stella’s care is the ward nurse, Barb (Kimberly Herbert Gregory), who runs a tight ship, insisting that her charges remain six feet apart. Always. Or risk contracting from another CF patient a lethal microbe called B.cepacia. It’s on the ward that Haley meets Will Newman (Cole Sprouse), also newly arrived, and also hooked up to an oxygen tank. Like Stella, he has CF and is in the hospital to participate in a clinical drug trial. When they first meet it’s oil and water, with an overlay of chemistry. Stella studiously ignores him and his questions, with a dash of salt, which, in Stella speak, means that Cole Sprouse and Haley Lu Richardson star in Five Feet Apart. she finds him interesting. So, they circle one another while stalked by their medical reality that frames their days – at times oppressively so. She is structured and obsessively organized and is on a lung transplant list. Will, whose disease is a bit more advanced and is therefore disqualified for a transplant, resists the drug trial, the meds, and the intrusiveness of his treatment. He would rather sketch or sit outside on the edge of the hospital roof, looking out at the horizon. Given all that is mentioned above, Five Feet Apart is essentially a charming romance. A love story. And therefore, like all such tales, there are exigent circumstances that must be overcome if a relationship is to bloom. Those barriers are expressed in the admonition by nurse Barb that Stella and Will cannot violate the six-foot rule. Their lives depend on it and they will not die on her watch. Naturally, they whittle it down to five feet, which is about the length of a pool stick, one actually carried around by Stella. I found the writing to be excellent – even with a dash of melodrama in act three – and the performances by Richardson and Sprouse extraordinary. They each inhabit their characters fully, especially Richardson who is radiant, her portrayal heartfelt and will definitely draw the tween/teen demographic into her and Will’s world. The sustained struggle of both Stella and Will is to survive another day. They face a reality that dictates that every breath they take is framed by a constant awareness that it requires effort and that what is almost a cliché – life is short – is a truth to be faced every day and is never an abstraction. Five Feet Apart is also about courage. Remarkable courage. CF is an anvil placed on young shoulders, theirs to confront and this film resists any temptation to exploit this disease for fanciful fairytale outcomes. Five Feet Apart. Directed by Justin Baldoni. Starring Haley Lu Richardson, Cole Sprouse, Kimberly Herbert Gregory. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/Netflix/ Prime.

articles.text: A scene from Luck. Luck is a vibrant computer animated film about an 18-yearold girl named Sam Greenfield who has spent all of her life at the Summerland School For Girls orphanage, wishing year after year that she would find a “forever family.” Sadly, no one ever appeared and now Sam has aged out of the orphanage and must go out into the world and live on her own, meaning she has to say goodbye to her young friend Hazel (Adelynn Spoon) who also hopes daily that a “forever family” will come to Summerland and take her home. Sam considers never having found a family as an example of being someone who has constant bad luck. Random objects fall on her, she slips and trips, and almost everything she touches breaks. So on her must-leave-Summerland day, she is driven to a new apartment by a cranky social worker who informs her that she can only visit Hazel on visitors’ day. She gets a job at Flowers & More, but on her first day, of course, oversleeps; her bathroom door sticks; and she drops her toast on the floor, jelly-side down; her bicycle tire has a flat, hence she arrives late for work. Her kind-hearted boss, Marv, tells her that the next day will be better, but does assign her to the cart patrol where she can’t wreck stuff. She also visits Hazel, but finds her despondent, still wishing for a family. Sam promises to bring her a lucky penny. Sam goes about settling in and visits a bustling café where she spots a black cat and begins to chat the critter up. And it’s while she’s there she spots a shiny penny and thinks of Hazel. Having the penny in her possession, things unexpectedly begin to go right: her socks match, the toast doesn’t fall upside down and the bathroom door opens with ease. But in a moment of bad timing she drops the penny in the toilet. She returns to the café looking for another penny, and encounters the same black cat that apparently can talk and tells her his name is Bob (Simon Pegg). The cat takes off through the streets and Sam follows and sees Bob pass through a strange portal. Sam is right behind Bob and discovers she is in a place called Land of Luck. And thus begins her very remarkable adventure. Land of Luck is filled with strange creatures: leprechauns, floating elevators, and even an anxiety-driven dragon (Jane Fonda). The head of Land of Luck is a woman named the Captain (Whoopi Goldberg). There are lots of surprises, and Sam does indeed learn a great deal about good luck and bad luck in the upside-down land, knowledge that she uses to help Hazel. Luck. Directed by Peggy Holmes. Skydance animated. With voices of Eva Noblezada, Simon Pegg, Whoopi Goldberg. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Apple tv+.

articles.text: Piedmont residents wanting a new community pool don’t have to hold their breath any longer. A groundbreaking ceremony for the city’s new community pool drew a crowd of hundreds on Saturday morning, December 17. Residents showed up in support and to applaud speeches from those most involved. Speakers at the groundbreaking ceremony included community members, and city official who have been working on building a new pool for more than 20 years, including resident Clarence Mamuyac, whose firm, ELS Architecture and Urban Design of Berkeley, was selected to design a new aquatic facility. “It’s a place to carve out a little bit of joy in our overcrowded and stressful schedule. That’s what this community pool means,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King. “This pool will change people’s lives. And for all of us here who supported measure UU, this is your legacy. I am so deeply appreciative.” she added. Hundreds of Pedometers braved the cold winter morning to formally acknowledged the beginning of pool construction.
articles.title: City rallies for groundbreaking of new community pool

articles.text: Swim practice was canceled last Saturday so that more than 100 members of the Piedmont Swim Team, their parents and coaches could converge at Piedmont Park for a photo prior to the groundbreaking ceremony of the new Piedmont Community Pool. “I’m super excited,” said Swim Teach coach Colby Price. ”It’s making everything a whole lot more real. The pool has been empty a long time, and it’s exciting to see that we are starting this project.” 11-year-old Amor Rodriguez has been on the swim team for eight months and while she loves the coaches and the team, she says having a home pool will make it even better. “I’m excited about the swimming pool because now we can have our own place to swim so we don’t have to go to different pools,” she said. “The new pool seems really cool, and I like it,” said Mason Armstrong. Nathan Judy said the swim team, provides him a sense of community and has become a second family for him. “We need a home pool right now. We’re a Piedmont swim team and we don’t have a pool. It would be nice to have one [within walking distance],” said Judy. Paige Arnold, who will be swimming for Amherst College next fall, was seven years old when she started swimming at the Piedmont Pool. She has fond memories of it being a fun community spot. While she was sad to see it close, she is looking forward to this next chapter. “I’m hoping that kids can have the same journey as mine; they’re at the age when I started swimming at the pool. I’m excited for them to have a community pool Young Piedmont Swim Team members Eva Stolicny (left) and Maia Saxena hold up their sign at the ceremony Photos by Lisa Carnazzo Event organizers acknowledged the large number of kids from the Piedmont Swim Team and asked them to have a photo taken. rather than going to Mills College and other pools.” Piedmont Swim Team member Zafar Majid said he misses the days when he could walk to swim practice right after school. “I’m excited about this new pool, because it takes a long time to drive to one pool and back. articles.text: It was another beautiful, cold, clear day last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. Melba Yee filled in for activity leader Dick Carter with a big group of 50 walkers and three K-9 best friends were on hand. Among the first-time walkers were local architect Rebecca Schnier, Phil Witte’s wife, and Joyce Bailey, a recent arrival to Piedmont. Piedmont architect and urban planner Will Adams led the walkers on a 1.6 mile loop on the familiar hilly streets around Exedra Plaza viewing and discussing the numerous architectural styles close to the center of town. These included Mission Revival, Craftsman, Victorian, Tudor, several Contemporary styles, Spanish Revival, Colonial Revival, and Art Nouveau. The group stopped at nine locations to review 12 buildings. It was astutely pointed out that there is an interesting richness to the city texture that results from so many different building styles. Some pointed out that what unites the different styles is the landscaping, especially the rows of mature street trees that connect and soften the differences of the buildings. The walk ended with the group being made privy by Will to a secret shortcut on their way back to the Exedra Plaza. On December 21 Melba Yee and Mike Henn will take the group down the hill to Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue for a holiday lunch. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: One of our favorite fall and winter fruit combinations is pears and cranberries. This cake speaks of the seasons and is welcomed on a dessert table for brunch, coffee or teatime, and dinner. I enjoy its simplicity but use your imagination on how to serve it according to the situation. A simple dusting of confectioner’s sugar or a dollop of softly whipped cream will go nicely. Or sliced as is won’t compromise its visual appeal. Choose either d’Anjou or Bosc pears if available, as they will hold up during the hour or so of baking, retaining both shape and some texture when fully baked. In comparison Bartlett pears can turn very soft and mushy. I usually load up on fresh cranberries as soon as I see them in stores. I keep a bag out for immediate use and toss the rest in the freezer, so cranberries are usually available at our house. If you don’t happen to have this small quantity on hand, substitute with raspberries or other fruit. Using frozen is fine, also. Pear Cranberry Cake Adapted from Back from Scratch INGREDIENTS • 1 cup unsalted butter, softened • 1 cup granulated sugar • 3 large eggs, room temperature • 2 cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 1/3 cup milk or half and half, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1/2 teaspoon almond extract • 1 large pear, d’Anjou or Bosc, cut into 12 wedges • 1/4 cup cranberries, whole • 1/4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the center position. Preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the sides and bottom of a 9-inch spring form pan. 2. In a small bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt. Set aside. 3. In a large mixing bowl, cream the softened butter and sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, 3 – 4 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add eggs, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Add vanilla and almond extracts and beat to incorporate. 4. Add about one-third of the flour mixture to the butter mixture, then half of the milk. Repeat with another one-third of the flour, the remaining milk, and finally the remaining flour; mixing just until combined after each addition. Do not over mix. 5. Transfer the batter into the prepared pan, smoothing the top to an even level. Arrange the pear slices in a decorative fashion, then distribute the cranberries. 6 Bake until lightly browned, about 30 minutes. Sprinkle with sliced almonds, and continue baking another 30 minutes, or until a wooden pick inserted in the center comes out clean. 7. Let cool in the pan for about 10 minutes, remove the sides of the springform and continue to cool slightly. The cake may be served warm or at room temperature. Add a dusting of confectioner’s sugar or softly whipped cream to serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Original published in the Piedmont Post on December 1, 2021

articles.text: On Saturday, December 17, Sacha Grippando, an independent jewelry appraiser and resident of Piedmont, gave an insightful and detailed talk at Piedmont Center for the Arts about jewelry from the Gilded Age. She began by outlining the history of the Gilded Age, talking about the rise of families like the Vanderbilts, Astors, Morgans and Rockefellers and how jewelry was used as a signifier of wealth and status. She went on to speak about the American heiresses or “dollar princesses” as they were referred to and how they brought their wealth to Europe, particularly to England, by marrying into old aristocratic and cash poor families who needed an injection of money to upkeep their massive ancestral palaces. She then moved on to talk about the highly influential coronations that occurred during this period that warranted the commissioning of some fabulous pieces of jewelry as well as how influential figures like Queen Alexandra and Maria Feodorovna, the Empress of Russia had on the style and types of jewelry that were popular. She also discussed the change in fashion from the voluminous hooped Victorian skirts to the tighter bustle dresses of the 1880s. She described how the evolution of fashion affected the types of jewelry that could be worn, and the rise of global luxury brands, Sothebys devant decorsage Sacha Grippando speaks at the Piedmont Center for the Arts about the jewelry from the Gilded Age. the notably Cartier, and their influence on the jewelry of the period. She recounted the humorous tale of how Cartier ended up with their flagship American store on 653 5th Avenue by swapping it for two strands of natural pearls. The next section of the talk focused on the jewelry; the manufacture, choice of gemstones and precious metals and the types that were popular. She examined the enormous effect of the Diamond Rush in South Africa in the late 19th century thus creating an abundance of diamonds on the market. She also discussed innovations made in metalsmithing and the rise in the use of platinum as well as talking about innovations in diamond cutting. She concluded with a discussion of the famous Hope diamond and its illustrious Gilded Age owner, the socialite and heiress Evalyn Walsh McLean. The lecture provided a delightful overview of a period of time that glittered and sparkled through the amazing jewelry that was created and worn. Grippando plans to host more jewelry lectures in 2023. The next one will be on jewelry from the Art Deco period.

articles.text: Is your New Year’s resolution to be more sustainable in 2023? Here are eight actions you can take to lower your carbon footprint this year! 1. Go zero waste: Swap out single-use items in your home for reusable or zero waste options. In the kitchen, you can exchange plastic wrap for beeswax wrap and zip-top bags for reusable silicone bags. Make the switch to eco-friendly and low-waste personal hygiene products. For example, try using a bamboo toothbrush or a shampoo bar. Check out nearby refill stores like Fillgood and Re-Up to get started today. 2. Start Composting: When organic waste decomposes in a landfill without oxygen, it produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. By composting your food scraps, you can easily reduce your ecological footprint. Piedmont residents can request a free 1.5-gallon kitchen scrap pail by emailing sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov. 3. Electrify your home: Here in Piedmont, residential buildings account for nearly half of in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. articles.text: Starting on Tuesday, January 3, 2023, the City of Piedmont will offer rebates for the removal of existing gas appliances and for their replacement with certain electric appliances. Rebates will be available for single family and multi-family properties. Eligible low-income applicants may qualify for additional funding. Rebates will only be issued for existing buildings; new construction is not eligible for this program. Rebates can be applied to equipment and installation labor for projects applying for a Building Permit on or after January 3. Here are some frequently asked questions about the program: Why is the City of Piedmont offering this program? The City is offering this rebate program to incentivize homeowners to electrify their homes. Building electrification has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont and help meet the City’s goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, as set by the Piedmont Climate Action Plan 2.0, which is available at bit. ly/3FI54mE. Will installing electric appliances increase monthly utility bills? The exact costs and savings will vary depending on your individual situation. Switching from a gas to electric-powered appliance may increase your electricity bill, while decreasing your gas bill. Nonetheless, using an efficient heat pump can lower your heating bills dramatically, especially in Piedmont where winters do not get too cold. If I can only afford to make one change, which appliance would be best for me to swap out first? As with many things, it depends on your home and your energy use. Traditionally, heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems (HVAC) are often the biggest energy consumers, followed by water heating systems. It also may be best to swap out the oldest appliance that is most in need of being replaced. Are there any additional or hidden costs to electrification? Besides the labor and appliance cost there may be costs to upgrade your home’s electrical system, depending on its age and condition. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security, says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. articles.text: If you’re a Boomer grandparent and your child is a Millennial parent, you’ve no doubt noticed one or two differences between your parenting style and your child’s style. In many families, these differences can be a source of friction, and that friction can effectively drain much of the joy out of family time. Does it need to be this way? What steps can a grandparent take to improve the situation? Childrearing recommendations have never been static. Parenting norms change with the times and reflect both new factual information from medical and psychological experts, as well as societal changes and cultural developments that influence family life. So, in the broad sense, societal shifts in parenting rules and recommendations have reasonable explanations; they can be explained by new data, medical advice, and community trends. For an individual family welcoming a new baby, however, these societal shifts can cause little tremors that can shake a Boomer grandparent’s expectations of what this time of their life was going to look like. For the Millennial new parent, the effort to bring their parents to a place of understanding and acceptance can be exhausting. Can’t we all just get along? What’s stopping us? Why is it hard for a grandparent who raised their children in the freewheeling 80’s or 90’s to accept that their adult children are raising their own children quite differently? Millennial parents strongly believe in validating childhood emotions, supporting a child’s independent choices, and tend to stress acceptance and tolerance over shame. Your grandchildren may be breast fed for two or more years, sleep at specific times and always with a sound machine, have limited time in front of screens, eat nothing but farm fresh organic foods, and be asked their opinion on absolutely everything from whether or not they want a hug, to what they want to wear to school, to how they want their sandwich cut. Boomers might not get this. But, why does it matter? Why do you feel it necessary to say to your grandchild’s parents: It seems so odd that you do X. Why don’t you do Y like I did? You turned out just fine, didn’t you? The world today looks nothing like the world you raised your children in. You had far fewer resources to learn from and fewer competing bits of information to analyze. Many of the skills that you taught your children simply aren’t needed anymore and you may be completely ignorant about many of the skills they need today. Your adult children are not criticizing what you did in raising them. They just want to do it their way with all of the information they now have. What if you asked yourself: What am I willing to do to ensure future happiness and harmony with my family? What if you actually asked yourself that question every time you were tempted to point out what seems odd or ill-advised to your adult child? What if you thought about how a seemingly innocent comment or question may come across to them? Take some time to ask yourself how you want to be remembered after you’re gone. Do you want to be remembered as the grandparent who had to be right all the time, who had to win or come out on top every time there was a discussion, or whose advice had to be followed otherwise you felt disrespected? Grandparenthood is your chance to lead by example, to be a role model, to be the wise elder. It’s the time that you can celebrate the successes of the younger generation in your family, and be there as a safety net in times of real challenge. You can decide to be a lifelong learner, and watch your grandchildren grow while trusting your adult children to know what is best for them. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. articles.text: All Aboard! Piedmont Seniors are about to board the train from the Jelly Belly factory in Fairfield to its newly opened museum. Pictured are Penny Robb, Carole Jones, Greg Jurin, Mona Jamieson, Sandra Curach, Irene Westler, Yorkman Lowe, Martin Rosson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Jim Ayotte, and Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. On November 9, a group of Piedmont Seniors was eager to get a head start on the holiday shopping frenzy. They visited the Vacaville Outlet stores with dozens of stores eager to welcome the group. The stores even offer a Senior discount upon request. After they were shopped out, the group had a filling lunch at Black Bear Diner in Vacaville, where they particularly enjoyed huckleberry ice cream. The last stop of the day was a visit the recently remodeled Jelly Belly Factory in nearby Fairfield, complete with a new museum. The Jelly Belly Factory has an interesting history. Formerly called the Herman Goetlitz Candy Company, the company, founded in 1919, moved from Oregon to Oakland on 61st Street near Emeryville in 1922. The company’s growth accelerated quickly after it sent its jelly bellies to California Governor Ronald Reagan to sample. Reagan was trying to quit smoking and decided that eating candy was a better alternative. Reagan even used to place these now-famous candies on conference tables for all his meetings, and after becoming President, he had a bowl of jelly beans in the suites at Blair House, Washington D.C.’s guest residence. The Jelly Belly factory offers daily self-guided walking tours where visitors can learn all about making jelly beans. Jelly Bellies were first produced in 1976. There is an attractive café for casual dining, where you will find jelly bean-shaped hamburgers and pizzas. The inviting gift shop has a huge assortment of all different kinds of candies. The factory routinely ships its jelly beans to all corners of the world. After shopping at the Jelly Belly store they took a short ride on the Jelly Belly Express to the newly opened museum, part of every tour. It recently opened and has large decorative jelly beans hanging from the ceiling. The museum shows the evolution of candy making equipment from 100 years ago to the present day, where robots do much of the work. All in all, the Piedmont Seniors had a very fun-filled outing. The group’s next excursion will be to the Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills on Wednesday, January 11, 2023. To participate in Piedmont Seniors activities, including monthly meetings at the Piedmont Community Hall, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov for further information, or call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510- 420-3070.
